What exactly do you do in a jury that would nullify ? Do you just day I hereby nullify, or do you have to get ththe other jurors to agree, or how does that work?

You declare not guilty.

Guilty verdict must be unanimous. End of story.

You can always vote to acquit no matter the evidence and the law. This happens during deliberations. If you can convince the other jurors, then the defendant will be acquitted and go free. If you can’t convince the others, the jury will be deadlocked, and a mistrial will be declared. In the case of a mistrial, the defendant can be re-tried, but that doesn’t always happen. If you are the lone-holdout, there’s a good chance of being retried.

So you have to convince the other jurors that the person should be acquitted despite the law and facts. Depending on the charges and the other jurors this might be relatively easy or extremely difficult.

The odds go down for the prosecution each time they retry a case. Prosecutors know this. I used to work with a deputy prosecutor in the Army Reserve, he despised being handed cases for retrial. Prosecutors like their success rate to be high, a plea deal is still a win in their book. They get very generous after a hung jury. Besides Jury trials are very expensive for the State.

It’s true that cases are expensive to take to trial and the state is reluctant to re-try cases after hung juries. However, the one huge exception is when the jury is hung due to nullification. Depending on the issues at play, a lone-holdout nullification is about the only time the state will be in a hurry to re-try the case. So while I agree with what you’ve said, the specific thing we’re discussing tends to be the exception unless you can convince a few other jurors to vote along with you. But if you can convince one or two you can hopefully convince them all and get a straight acquittal.
